statement: Written rules for physical and logical access to information and assets are set, based on business and security needs such as need-to-know and least privilege. The rules are applied in real access configurations through role-based groups and by avoiding shared admin accounts. The access policy and system access listings are the proof.
why_asked: Access that grows without a rule becomes broad and hard to defend. Policy that does not match actual settings gives false comfort.
how_to_ask: Ask for the access policy, then ask to see how two systems are actually configured. Example probe: "Show me who can reach the finance system and which rule says they should."
question: Does your organization apply rules for physical and logical access based on its business needs?
expected_evidence: Access control policy covering logical and physical access; system access listings and role or group definitions for sampled systems; list of shared or generic accounts and exceptions. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The policy states access principles and who decides. Sampled systems use role or group access that matches the rules, with no shared admin accounts or documented exceptions.
test: Read the access policy for logical and physical rules grounded in business and security needs. Sample systems and compare access listings with the rules. Pass if the policy is approved and all sampled systems follow the rules.
baseline_risk: Access is granted ad hoc, so people hold more access than they need and no one can justify it.

statement: Creation, change and removal of identities are managed, each identity is linked to one person or to an owned non-person account, and shared identities are controlled. Active accounts are reconciled against the HR roster on a defined cycle so departed staff have no active identity, and every service account has an assigned owner. Reconciliation records and the account list are the proof.
why_asked: Orphaned accounts of leavers and ownerless service accounts are a common route for misuse and are rarely noticed.
how_to_ask: Ask how a new starter gets an account and how a leaver's account disappears. Ask for the last reconciliation. Example probe: "Compare this identity export with the HR leaver list. Are any leavers still active?"
question: Does your organization manage the full life cycle of identities, linking each to an accountable owner and removing those of leavers?
expected_evidence: Identity management procedure; identity provider account export; HR roster and leaver list; reconciliation records; service account list with named owners. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The procedure covers creation, change and removal, and limits shared identities. Reconciliation shows no active identity for departed staff. Every service account has an owner.
test: Reconcile the identity provider export with the HR roster and leaver list for the audit period, and sample service accounts. Pass if no leaver has an active identity and all sampled service accounts have a recorded owner.
baseline_risk: Former staff or unowned accounts stay active and can be used without anyone being accountable.

statement: Issuing, resetting and revoking of authentication credentials such as passwords, tokens and keys are controlled, with identity verified before any reset. Users receive written guidance on keeping credentials confidential, and default vendor credentials are changed when systems are installed. The procedure, user guidance and build checks are the proof.
why_asked: Weak reset processes let attackers take over accounts, and default passwords on new systems are among the first things attackers try.
how_to_ask: Ask how a password reset request is verified and how new systems are built. Ask for a build checklist. Example probe: "A user calls saying they are locked out. What do you do before you reset anything?"
question: Does your organization control how authentication credentials are issued, reset, revoked and kept safe by users?
expected_evidence: Credential issue, reset and revocation procedure; user guidance on credential confidentiality; awareness training records covering it; build checklists or configuration baselines showing default credentials changed. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: A procedure covers issue, reset and revocation, with identity checks before reset. Users have written guidance. Build records show default credentials changed.
test: Read the procedure and user guidance. Sample recent resets and check identity was verified. Sample new systems and check build records show default credentials were changed. Pass if all sampled resets were verified and all sampled builds changed defaults.
baseline_risk: Accounts are taken over through social engineering at reset or through unchanged default passwords.

statement: Access is requested and approved by someone with the authority to grant it before it is granted or changed, and in line with the access rules. Access is provisioned only against an approved request. Request tickets with approvals are the proof.
why_asked: Access given on a verbal ask or without approval accumulates quietly and bypasses the rules.
how_to_ask: Ask for a few recent access requests from start to finish and check approval comes before the grant. Example probe: "Pick a user who gained admin rights this quarter. Show me the request and when it was approved compared with when it was granted."
question: Does your organization grant or change access only after documented approval and in line with the access rules?
expected_evidence: Access request and approval procedure; access request tickets with approval and timestamps; list of access grants and changes for the period; list of who may approve access. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The policy requires a request and approval before provisioning. Every grant or change traces to an approved request that came first, given by someone with authority to approve.
test: Sample new or changed access grants from the audit period and find the approval record for each. Pass if every sampled grant has an approval dated before the access was given.
baseline_risk: People gain access without anyone with authority agreeing to it.

statement: Access rights for in-scope systems are reviewed on a defined cycle, and access that is no longer appropriate is removed. Each review records what was checked, the decisions and the removals, and completion of removals is confirmed. Completed review records are the proof.
why_asked: Over time people change role and keep old access. Without a review, rights creep and no one notices.
how_to_ask: Ask for the review schedule and the last completed review. Check removals were actually carried out. Example probe: "In your last review, how many accounts were removed and where is the proof they were?"
question: Does your organization review access rights at a set frequency and remove access that is no longer appropriate?
expected_evidence: Access review procedure and schedule; completed user access review records for in-scope systems; evidence that removals were completed; reviewer sign-offs. Cover the last two review cycles.
good_looks_like: Reviews take place at the defined frequency for every in-scope system. Each review is done by someone with authority over that system. Inappropriate access found is removed and the removal confirmed.
test: Check the schedule against completed reviews for in-scope systems over the audit period. Sample removals recommended in the reviews and confirm each was carried out. Pass if every in-scope system was reviewed on time and all sampled removals are confirmed.
baseline_risk: Excess and outdated access stays in place and is used to cause or hide harm.

statement: Access is removed or adjusted when people leave or change role, within the timeframe the policy sets. Each leaver or move is notified from the HR process, and the time access ended is recorded. Leaver lists and identity provider logs are the proof.
why_asked: Access left open after someone leaves or moves lets former staff and old duties persist, which is a leading cause of insider incidents.
how_to_ask: Ask what triggers removal and how fast. Compare HR dates with account end dates. Example probe: "Take your last leaver. When did they finish, and when did their access actually stop?"
question: Does your organization remove or adjust access promptly when people leave or change role, within the timeframe it has set?
expected_evidence: Leaver and mover procedure with the removal timeframe; HR leaver and role change list; identity provider logs showing disablement dates; access removal tickets. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: A stated timeframe applies to leavers and movers. A leaver or move notice triggers removal. Logs show access ended within the timeframe for every sampled person.
test: Sample leavers and role changes from the audit period. Compare HR end or move dates with identity provider logs. Pass if every sampled person lost or changed access within the timeframe in the policy.
baseline_risk: Former staff or people in new roles retain access they should not have.

statement: Duties that conflict, such as requesting and approving access, or developing and deploying to production, are identified and held by different people. System roles or approval workflows enforce the separation. Where it is not feasible, a compensating measure such as monitoring or supervisory review is documented. The conflict list and role assignments are the proof.
why_asked: One person holding both sides of a sensitive task can commit or hide fraud or error alone.
how_to_ask: Ask for the list of conflicting duties and then ask to see two examples in system roles or approvals. For small teams, ask for the compensating measure. Example probe: "Can the person who raises a production change also approve and deploy it?"
question: Does your organization separate conflicting duties, or apply compensating measures where separation is not possible?
expected_evidence: List of conflicting duties and role definitions; role assignments or approval records showing different people for each side; documented compensating measures with monitoring or review records; risk assessment covering exceptions. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: Conflicting pairs are identified and assigned to different people through system roles or approval workflows. Exceptions have documented compensating measures that are actually performed.
test: Take the list of conflicting duty pairs and sample each pair in role assignments or approval records. Pass if different individuals hold each side in every sample, or a documented compensating measure was performed.
baseline_risk: A single person can perform and conceal a harmful action without a second check.

statement: Privileged access is authorized separately from standard access, limited to people who need it and held in accounts separate from everyday use. A current list of privileged accounts is kept with a recorded authorization for each, and privileged access is reviewed on a defined cycle, removing unneeded rights. The account list and review records are the proof.
why_asked: Privileged accounts give the keys to systems, so one stolen or misused account can cause a total compromise.
how_to_ask: Ask for the list of privileged accounts and how it is built. Ask if admins use separate accounts for email. Example probe: "Show me the domain administrators, who approved each, and when the group was last reviewed."
question: Does your organization authorize, limit, record and regularly review privileged access rights, held in accounts separate from everyday use?
expected_evidence: Privileged access policy; current privileged account list with authorization records; evidence of separate admin accounts; privileged access review records. Cover the last two review cycles.
good_looks_like: A current list names every privileged account holder with a recorded authorization. Admin rights sit in separate accounts. Reviews remove unneeded rights and occur more often than standard reviews where the policy says so.
test: Compare the privileged account list with the groups and roles in the systems, then sample holders and find the authorization for each. Check that a privileged review took place in the audit period. Pass if the list matches the systems, all sampled holders are authorized and the review is complete.
baseline_risk: Excess administrator rights let one compromised or careless account take over systems and data.

statement: Access controls are configured in each system by role or group so users reach only the information and functions their role allows, in line with the access rules. Sampled users are tested to confirm they cannot go beyond their role. Role matrices and test results are the proof.
why_asked: A good policy does not matter if systems let users see or do more than their role requires. This control checks the system itself.
how_to_ask: Ask for the role matrix for a key system and then test it. Example probe: "Log in as a standard user and try to open the payroll function. What happens?"
question: Does your organization restrict access to information and functions in each system to what each role is authorized to use?
expected_evidence: System role or group matrices for in-scope applications; access listings for sampled users; access test results; access control policy. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: Each in-scope system has roles that map to job needs. Testing shows users cannot reach information or functions outside their role.
test: Sample in-scope systems and users and try to reach information and functions outside each user's role. Pass if every attempt is denied and role settings match the matrix.
baseline_risk: Users see or change information and functions they have no business need for.

statement: Who may read and write source code repositories, build tools and software libraries is defined, and write access is limited to authorized developers. Protected branches require review before changes merge. Repository permission exports are the proof.
why_asked: Anyone who can change code or build tools can slip in a flaw or backdoor that reaches production.
how_to_ask: Ask for repository permissions and branch protection settings on the main repositories. Example probe: "Can a developer push straight to the production branch without a review?"
question: Does your organization limit access to source code and build tools to authorized people, with review before changes merge?
expected_evidence: Secure development policy rules on code access; repository permission export; branch protection settings; build tool access list. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: Rules name who may read and write each repository and tool. Permissions limit write access to authorized developers. Protected branches require review before merge.
test: Sample repositories, including the most critical, and review permission exports and branch protection settings. Pass if write access is limited to authorized developers and review is required before merge in every sampled repository.
baseline_risk: Unauthorized or unreviewed changes enter code and build tools and reach production.
applicability: Applies if the organization develops or customizes software in house.

statement: Authentication strength is set by system sensitivity, requiring multi-factor authentication for remote, privileged and sensitive-data access, and is enforced in the identity provider or systems. Log-on protections such as lockout or throttling after failed attempts are configured. Policy settings and configuration exports are the proof.
why_asked: Stolen or guessed passwords are the most common way in. Multi-factor authentication and lockout stop most of these attacks.
how_to_ask: Ask which systems require multi-factor authentication and who is exempt. Ask for the identity provider policy export. Example probe: "Show me an administrator who logs in without multi-factor authentication, if one exists, and why."
question: Does your organization enforce authentication strength by system sensitivity, including multi-factor where needed, and protect log-on against guessing?
expected_evidence: Authentication standard by system sensitivity; identity provider configuration export showing multi-factor and lockout settings; list of exceptions with approvals; configuration baselines. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The standard sets required methods by sensitivity. The identity provider enforces multi-factor for remote, privileged and sensitive access. Lockout or throttling is on. Exceptions are approved and rare.
test: Review the identity provider export and sample remote, privileged and sensitive-system accounts. Pass if every sampled account is covered by the required methods, lockout or throttling is configured and every exception is approved.
baseline_risk: Accounts are broken into with stolen or guessed passwords.

statement: Utility programs that can override system or application controls are identified, and their use is limited to named, authorized people. Every use of those utilities is logged and authorizations are kept. The utility list, access settings and logs are the proof.
why_asked: Utilities such as disk editors or admin consoles can bypass normal controls, so uncontrolled use leaves no trace of misuse.
how_to_ask: Ask which tools are able to bypass controls and who may run them. Ask for logs of their use. Example probe: "Who ran the database admin utility last month, and who approved it?"
question: Does your organization restrict utility programs that can override system or application controls to authorized people and log their use?
expected_evidence: List of override-capable utility programs; access settings or allow lists; authorization records; utility usage logs. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The utilities are identified and restricted to named people. Use is logged and tied to an authorization.
test: Take the utility list and check access settings limit each to named people. Sample logged uses from the audit period and find the authorization for each. Pass if only named people can use the utilities and all sampled uses are logged with an authorization.
baseline_risk: Staff or attackers bypass system controls with tools that leave no record.
